stem: The climate of India is broadly described as the __________ type of climate.
solution: The climate of India is broadly described as the 'monsoon' type (tropical monsoon) climate. The word 'monsoon' (from the Arabic 'mausim', meaning season) refers to the seasonal reversal of the wind direction through the year — and India's climate is dominated by this monsoon rhythm, with a rainy summer season (when moist winds blow from the sea to the land) and a dry winter season (when dry winds blow from the land to the sea). So India has a monsoon climate. Understanding that India has a monsoon type of climate is a fundamental prelims point. India has a monsoon (tropical monsoon) type of climate.

stem: The word 'monsoon' is derived from the Arabic word 'mausim', which means:
solution: The word 'monsoon' is derived from the Arabic word 'mausim', which means 'season'. This reflects the essential nature of the monsoon: it is a seasonal phenomenon — the winds reverse their direction with the seasons (blowing from the sea to the land in the summer/wet season, and from the land to the sea in the winter/dry season). So the monsoon is fundamentally about the seasonal change of winds. Understanding the meaning of 'monsoon' (from 'mausim' = season) is a prelims point. 'Monsoon' comes from the Arabic 'mausim', meaning season.

stem: The monsoon winds are essentially winds that reverse their direction:
solution: The monsoon winds are winds that reverse (change) their direction seasonally — between summer and winter. In summer, the moist 'south-west monsoon' blows from the sea (the Indian Ocean/Arabian Sea/Bay of Bengal) toward the land, bringing heavy rainfall; in winter, the dry 'north-east monsoon' blows from the land toward the sea. This seasonal reversal of the wind direction is the defining feature of the monsoon, and it gives India its distinct wet and dry seasons. Understanding that monsoon winds reverse seasonally is a key prelims point. The monsoon winds reverse their direction seasonally, between summer and winter.

stem: The main cause of the Indian monsoon is the differential heating of __________ between summer and winter.
solution: The main cause of the Indian monsoon is the differential heating (and cooling) of the land and the sea between summer and winter. In summer, the land (the vast Asian landmass) heats up much more than the sea, creating a low-pressure area over the land (especially north-western India/Asia), which draws in moist air from the higher-pressure sea (the south-west summer monsoon). In winter, the reverse happens: the land cools more than the sea, forming a high-pressure area over the land, from which dry air blows out toward the sea (the north-east winter monsoon). So the unequal heating of land and sea, and the resulting pressure differences, drive the seasonal reversal of the monsoon winds. (Other factors — like the shift of the ITCZ, the Himalayas, the Tibetan Plateau, and jet streams — also play a role.) Understanding that the differential heating of land and sea causes the monsoon is a key prelims point. The Indian monsoon is caused mainly by the differential heating of the land and the sea between summer and winter.

stem: The rain-bearing summer monsoon of India, which brings most of the country's rainfall, is the __________ monsoon.
solution: The rain-bearing summer monsoon of India is the south-west monsoon. It blows from the south-west (from the Indian Ocean and the Arabian Sea/Bay of Bengal) toward the land during the summer (roughly June to September). Because it comes from over the warm seas, it is laden with moisture, and it brings the bulk (about 75–90%) of India's annual rainfall. Its arrival ('the bursting of the monsoon') in June is eagerly awaited, as Indian agriculture depends heavily on it. Understanding that the south-west monsoon brings India's summer rains is a key prelims point. The south-west monsoon is the rain-bearing summer monsoon that brings most of India's rainfall.

stem: The south-west monsoon usually reaches (bursts over) the southern tip of India (Kerala) around:
solution: The south-west monsoon usually reaches (bursts over) the southern tip of India — the Kerala coast — around the 1st of June (the beginning of June). From there, it advances northward and across the country over the following weeks, covering the whole of India by about mid-July. The sudden onset of the monsoon, with a big change to heavy rain, is called the 'burst' of the monsoon. (The monsoon then begins to withdraw/retreat from about September.) Understanding that the monsoon reaches Kerala around 1st June is a prelims point. The south-west monsoon reaches the Kerala coast around 1st June.

stem: The south-west monsoon splits into two branches over India: the Arabian Sea branch and the __________ branch.
solution: As the south-west monsoon advances, it splits into two branches because of the shape of the Indian peninsula: (1) the Arabian Sea branch, which strikes the western coast (the Western Ghats) and brings heavy rain to the west coast and, moving inland, to much of central and northern India; and (2) the Bay of Bengal branch, which moves up the Bay of Bengal and strikes the north-eastern region and the Ganga plains (deflected by the mountains toward the west along the plains). Understanding the two branches of the south-west monsoon (Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal) is a prelims point. The south-west monsoon splits into the Arabian Sea branch and the Bay of Bengal branch.

stem: The Western Ghats cause very heavy rainfall on the western (coastal) side of India because they force the Arabian Sea branch of the monsoon to rise — an example of __________ rainfall.
solution: The Western Ghats cause very heavy rainfall on their western (windward, coastal) side because they act as a barrier, forcing the moisture-laden Arabian Sea branch of the south-west monsoon to rise up their slopes; as this air rises, it cools and its moisture condenses, giving heavy rain — this is orographic (relief) rainfall. The west coast (like the Konkan and Malabar coasts) therefore gets very heavy monsoon rain, while the leeward eastern side (the Deccan interior) lies in a rain shadow and is much drier. Understanding that the Western Ghats cause orographic rainfall is a prelims point. The Western Ghats force the monsoon to rise, causing heavy orographic (relief) rainfall on the west coast.

stem: One of the wettest places on Earth, receiving extremely heavy monsoon rainfall, is __________ (in Meghalaya).
solution: Mawsynram (and nearby Cherrapunji/Sohra), in the Khasi Hills of Meghalaya (north-eastern India), is one of the wettest places on Earth. It receives extremely heavy rainfall (often over 1000 cm / 11,000 mm a year) because the Bay of Bengal branch of the south-west monsoon is funnelled up the steep, funnel-shaped Khasi Hills, forcing the moist air to rise sharply and give intense orographic rainfall. This is a striking example of India's rainfall extremes. Understanding that Mawsynram/Cherrapunji is among the world's wettest places is a prelims point. Mawsynram/Cherrapunji, in Meghalaya, is one of the wettest places on Earth.

stem: The driest part of India, receiving very little rainfall, is the __________ region (in Rajasthan).
solution: The driest part of India is the Thar Desert region (in western Rajasthan), which receives very little rainfall (generally less than 25 cm a year). This region is dry because it lies away from the main path of the moisture-bearing monsoon branches, and the Aravalli Hills lie parallel to the Arabian Sea branch (so they do not force it to rise and give rain), while by the time the monsoon reaches there it has lost most of its moisture. So the Thar is arid, in contrast to the very wet north-east and west coast. Understanding that the Thar Desert is the driest part of India is a prelims point. The Thar Desert (western Rajasthan) is the driest part of India, receiving very little rainfall.

stem: The season during which the south-west monsoon 'retreats' or withdraws from India (roughly September to November) is called the __________ monsoon season.
solution: The retreating monsoon season (also called the post-monsoon or the season of the retreating monsoon) is the transition season, roughly from September to November, when the south-west monsoon weakens and withdraws (retreats) from India — first from the north-west, and progressively from the rest of the country. During this season, the weather is generally clear and the days are warm (with high humidity — 'October heat'). Importantly, this is also the season when the retreating monsoon picks up moisture over the Bay of Bengal and brings rainfall to the Coromandel coast (Tamil Nadu), and when tropical cyclones often strike the eastern coast. Understanding the retreating monsoon season (Sept–Nov) is a prelims point. The retreating monsoon season (roughly September–November) is when the south-west monsoon withdraws from India.

stem: The Coromandel coast (Tamil Nadu) receives most of its rainfall in winter (October–December) from the:
solution: The Coromandel coast (the coast of Tamil Nadu and southern Andhra Pradesh) is unusual in that it receives most of its rainfall in the winter months (October to December), from the retreating (north-east) monsoon. During the retreating monsoon season, the winds blow from the north-east, from the land toward the sea; but as they cross over the Bay of Bengal, they pick up moisture, and on striking the Coromandel coast (and being helped by cyclones), they give this coast its main rainy season in winter — while most of the rest of India is dry then. Understanding that the Coromandel coast gets winter rain from the retreating (NE) monsoon is a prelims point. The Coromandel coast gets most of its rain in winter from the retreating (north-east) monsoon.

stem: In the cold weather (winter) season, north-western India receives some rainfall from the __________, which are low-pressure systems coming from the Mediterranean region.
solution: In the winter (cold weather) season, north-western India (Punjab, Haryana, and the western Himalayas) receives some rainfall (and snowfall in the mountains) from 'western disturbances'. These are low-pressure weather systems (extra-tropical cyclones/depressions) that originate over the Mediterranean Sea region and travel eastward, across West Asia, to reach north-western India, bringing light winter rain to the plains and snow to the mountains. This winter rain, though small in amount, is very important for the 'rabi' (winter) crops, especially wheat. Understanding western disturbances (bringing winter rain to NW India) is a prelims point. Western disturbances are Mediterranean low-pressure systems that bring winter rainfall to north-western India.

stem: The hot, dry, dusty local wind that blows over the northern plains of India during the summer (hot weather season) is called the:
solution: The 'Loo' is the hot, dry, dusty, and often strong local wind that blows over the northern plains of India (from the west and north-west) during the hot weather (summer) season (May and June). Blowing during the daytime, it can be scorching and is dangerous to health (causing heat strokes / 'sunstroke'). It is an example of the extreme heat of the north Indian summer before the monsoon breaks. Understanding the Loo (India's hot summer wind) is a prelims point. The Loo is the hot, dry, dusty wind that blows over the northern plains of India in summer.

stem: The localised, violent thunderstorms with strong winds and heavy rain that occur in the eastern and north-eastern parts of India (Bengal, Assam) in the pre-monsoon (summer) season are called:
solution: Nor'westers are the localised, violent thunderstorms — with strong (often destructive) winds, thunder, lightning, and heavy rain (sometimes hail) — that occur in the eastern and north-eastern parts of India (West Bengal, Assam, and neighbouring areas) during the pre-monsoon (hot) season (April–May). In West Bengal, they are called 'Kalbaisakhi' (the 'calamity of the month of Baisakh'). Though violent, they are beneficial for tea, jute, and rice crops. (In Assam, they are called 'Bardoli Chheerha'.) Understanding the Nor'westers/Kalbaisakhi (pre-monsoon thunderstorms of eastern India) is a prelims point. Nor'westers (Kalbaisakhi) are the violent pre-monsoon thunderstorms of eastern and north-eastern India.

stem: The pre-monsoon showers in Kerala and Karnataka (in April–May) that are helpful for the ripening of mangoes and coffee are locally called:
solution: Mango showers are the pre-monsoon showers of rain that fall in Kerala and coastal Karnataka (and parts of the south) in April and May (before the arrival of the main south-west monsoon). They are so called because they are helpful for the ripening of mangoes (and are also called 'blossom showers' for their help to coffee blossoms/plantations in Karnataka). Understanding mango showers (pre-monsoon rains of the south, good for mangoes) is a prelims point. Mango showers are the pre-monsoon showers of Kerala and Karnataka that help ripen mangoes (and coffee).

stem: Indian agriculture is often described as a 'gamble on the monsoon' because:
options: The success of crops depends heavily on the monsoon rains, which are variable and uncertain (in timing and amount)
Rain is not needed for crops
solution: Indian agriculture is often described as a 'gamble on the monsoon' because it depends very heavily on the monsoon rains, which are variable, uncertain, and erratic — in their timing (they may arrive early or late), their duration, and their amount (some years bring too little rain — drought — and others too much — floods; and the rain is unevenly distributed). Since a large part of Indian farming is rain-fed (dependent on the monsoon), a good monsoon means good harvests, while a weak or failed monsoon can cause crop failure, drought, and hardship — so the fate of the crops (and much of the economy) 'gambles' on the behaviour of the monsoon each year. This is why irrigation and monsoon prediction are so important for India. Understanding why Indian agriculture is a 'gamble on the monsoon' is a prelims-relevant point. Indian agriculture is a 'gamble on the monsoon' because crops depend heavily on the variable, uncertain monsoon rains.

stem: The unifying influence of the monsoon on India is seen in the way it:
options: Ties the whole country together in a common rhythm of seasons and agricultural activity, and is eagerly awaited across the land
solution: The monsoon is regarded as a unifying influence on India because it ties the whole country together in a common seasonal rhythm and a shared way of life: the entire land waits for and depends on the monsoon; its arrival brings relief from the summer heat and sets in motion the agricultural activities (sowing, farming) all across the country; and it shapes a common annual cycle of seasons, festivals, and life for people everywhere in India. In this way, the monsoon binds the diverse regions and peoples of India into a unity, shaping a shared 'monsoon culture'. Understanding the monsoon's unifying influence is a prelims-relevant point. The monsoon is a unifying influence, tying the whole country together in a common rhythm of seasons and agricultural life.

stem: A major characteristic of monsoon rainfall in India is that it is __________ in its distribution (both over space and over time).
solution: A major characteristic of the monsoon rainfall in India is that it is uneven and variable — both over space (from region to region) and over time (from year to year, and within the season). Over space: some areas (like the north-east and the west coast) get extremely heavy rain, while others (like the Thar Desert and the leeward rain-shadow areas) get very little. Over time: the amount and timing of the rain vary greatly from year to year (some years too much, some too little), and the rain often comes in a few heavy spells with dry spells ('breaks') in between. This unevenness and unreliability of monsoon rainfall is a key feature (and a major challenge for India). Understanding the uneven, variable nature of monsoon rainfall is a prelims point. Monsoon rainfall in India is uneven and variable, in both its spatial distribution and its timing/amount from year to year.

stem: Assertion (A): The Western Ghats' windward (western) side is very wet, while the Deccan interior is much drier. Reason (R): The Western Ghats force the monsoon air to rise and drop its rain on the windward side, leaving a rain shadow on the leeward (eastern) side. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the windward (western) side of the Western Ghats is very wet, while the Deccan interior (to their east) is much drier. And the reason is (R) that the Western Ghats force the moisture-laden Arabian Sea branch of the monsoon to rise up their western slopes, where the air cools and drops most of its moisture as heavy orographic rain (making the windward west coast very wet); having lost its moisture, the air then descends the leeward (eastern) side, warming and drying, so the Deccan interior lies in a rain shadow and gets much less rain. So R correctly explains A. Understanding this orographic/rain-shadow effect of the Western Ghats is a prelims point. The Western Ghats' west side is wet and the Deccan drier because the Ghats force the monsoon to rain on the windward side, leaving a leeward rain shadow.

stem: India's climate is influenced by its latitude: the Tropic of Cancer divides the country into a __________ southern half and a __________ northern half.
solution: The Tropic of Cancer (23.5°N) passes through the middle of India, dividing it into a tropical southern half (which lies within the tropics, south of the Tropic of Cancer) and a sub-tropical northern half (which lies north of the Tropic of Cancer, in the sub-tropical zone). This is why the south of India is warmer and more uniformly hot through the year (tropical), while the north experiences a greater range of temperature, with cooler winters (sub-tropical/continental influence). Understanding that the Tropic of Cancer divides India into tropical and sub-tropical halves is a prelims point. The Tropic of Cancer divides India into a tropical southern half and a sub-tropical northern half.

stem: The main factors that control the climate of India include latitude, altitude, distance from the sea, relief (mountains), and:
options: the monsoon winds / pressure and wind systems (and jet streams, ocean currents)
solution: The main factors that control India's climate are: latitude (the Tropic of Cancer through the middle — tropical south, sub-tropical north); altitude (highlands like the Himalayas are cold); distance from the sea / continentality (coastal areas equable, interiors extreme); relief (mountains — the Himalayas act as a climatic barrier, and the Western Ghats cause orographic rain); and, crucially, the pressure and wind systems — especially the monsoon winds (and the upper-air jet streams, the shift of the ITCZ, and ocean phenomena like El Niño) — which govern the seasonal rhythm and the rainfall. Together these factors shape India's monsoon climate and its regional variations. Understanding the factors controlling India's climate is a prelims point. India's climate is controlled by latitude, altitude, distance from the sea, relief, and the monsoon/pressure-and-wind systems.

stem: The Himalayas influence India's climate by acting as a __________ that protects India from the cold, dry winds of Central Asia in winter.
solution: The Himalayas act as a great climatic barrier (a protective wall) for India: in winter, they block the extremely cold, dry winds that blow from Central Asia, preventing them from entering India — which is why northern India, although in similar latitudes, is much warmer in winter than Central Asia. The Himalayas also block the moisture-laden monsoon winds in summer, forcing them to shed their rain over India (rather than passing on), and thus help cause the heavy monsoon rainfall. So the Himalayas both shield India from cold and trap the monsoon rains — a major influence on India's climate. Understanding the Himalayas as a climatic barrier is a prelims point. The Himalayas act as a climatic barrier, blocking cold Central Asian winds in winter and trapping the monsoon rains.

stem: The shifting of the ITCZ (Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone) northward over India in summer helps to draw in the:
solution: The ITCZ (Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone) is the low-pressure belt near the equator where the trade winds converge. In the northern summer, as the Sun's overhead position shifts north (toward the Tropic of Cancer), the ITCZ also shifts northward over the Indian region, forming a zone of low pressure over northern India (the 'monsoon trough'). This northward-shifted low-pressure zone draws in the moist south-west monsoon winds (which are, in effect, the southern-hemisphere south-east trade winds that cross the equator and are drawn into this low, becoming the south-west monsoon). So the northward shift of the ITCZ in summer helps establish the south-west monsoon. Understanding the ITCZ's role in the monsoon is a prelims point. The northward shift of the ITCZ over India in summer helps draw in the south-west monsoon.

stem: The abnormal warming of the eastern Pacific Ocean known as El Niño is generally associated with a __________ monsoon in India.
solution: El Niño — the periodic abnormal warming of the surface waters of the central and eastern Pacific Ocean — is generally associated with a weak or deficient (below-normal) south-west monsoon in India, and hence an increased risk of drought. This is because the changes in atmospheric circulation during an El Niño tend to suppress the rising air and rainfall over the Indian region. (Its opposite phase, La Niña — the cooling of the eastern Pacific — is generally associated with a good/strong monsoon.) The El Niño–monsoon link is very important for forecasting India's rainfall. Understanding that El Niño weakens the Indian monsoon is a prelims point. El Niño is generally associated with a weak or deficient (drought-prone) monsoon in India.

stem: The 'Southern Oscillation' (SO) refers to the see-saw of atmospheric pressure between the eastern and western Pacific; together with El Niño it forms the phenomenon called:
solution: The 'Southern Oscillation' (SO) is the see-saw (periodic swinging) of atmospheric pressure between the eastern Pacific and the western Pacific/Indian Ocean region (when pressure is high on one side, it is low on the other, and this reverses periodically). The Southern Oscillation is closely linked with El Niño (the ocean-warming phenomenon), and together they form the coupled ocean-atmosphere phenomenon called ENSO (El Niño–Southern Oscillation). ENSO strongly affects the Indian monsoon and weather worldwide. A related index (the difference in pressure between Tahiti and Darwin) is used to predict the monsoon. Understanding ENSO (El Niño + Southern Oscillation) is a prelims point. ENSO (El Niño–Southern Oscillation) is the coupled phenomenon of El Niño and the Southern Oscillation, which affects the Indian monsoon.

stem: The upper-air westerly wind current that flows over India in winter and helps steer the western disturbances is the __________ jet stream.
solution: The subtropical westerly jet stream is a fast-flowing river of air in the upper atmosphere (troposphere) that flows from west to east over India (to the south of the Himalayas) during the winter. It plays an important role in India's winter weather: it helps to steer/bring the western disturbances (the Mediterranean low-pressure systems) into north-western India, giving winter rain. In summer, this westerly jet shifts north of the Himalayas (and an easterly jet appears over India). Understanding the subtropical westerly jet stream (winter, steers western disturbances) is a prelims point. The subtropical westerly jet stream flows over India in winter and helps steer the western disturbances.

stem: The upper-air easterly jet stream that develops over India in summer is thought to help in the __________ of the south-west monsoon.
solution: The tropical easterly jet stream is a fast upper-air current that flows from east to west over southern India (peninsular India) during the summer. Its development is linked to the onset (burst) of the south-west monsoon: as the subtropical westerly jet shifts north of the Himalayas in summer and the easterly jet establishes over India, conditions become favourable for the sudden onset of the monsoon. So the tropical easterly jet is associated with (and thought to help trigger) the burst of the south-west monsoon. Understanding the tropical easterly jet stream (summer, linked to monsoon onset) is a prelims point. The tropical easterly jet stream develops over India in summer and is linked to the onset (burst) of the south-west monsoon.

stem: The intense heating of the __________ Plateau in summer creates a strong low pressure that helps to strengthen/draw in the Indian monsoon.
solution: The intense heating of the Tibetan Plateau (a huge, high plateau to the north of the Himalayas) during the summer creates a strong region of low pressure and rising air (and an associated upper-air high) over it, which plays an important role in strengthening and drawing in the Indian summer monsoon. The heated Tibetan Plateau acts like a giant 'heat engine', reinforcing the low pressure over the region and the circulation that pulls in the moist south-west monsoon winds. Understanding the role of the Tibetan Plateau's heating in the monsoon is a prelims point. The intense summer heating of the Tibetan Plateau helps strengthen and draw in the Indian monsoon.

stem: A 'break' in the monsoon refers to:
options: The complete end of the monsoon
Dry spells (rainless periods) that occur within the rainy season, between wet spells
solution: A 'break' in the monsoon refers to the dry spells (rainless or low-rainfall periods) that occur within the rainy (monsoon) season, in between the wet spells of rain. The monsoon rainfall does not fall continuously through the season; rather, it comes in spells of heavy rain separated by these 'breaks' (dry intervals of a few days to weeks). The breaks are related to the movement of the monsoon trough and other conditions. Long breaks can harm crops (like a mini-drought within the rainy season). Understanding the 'break' in the monsoon (dry spells within the rainy season) is a prelims point. A 'break' in the monsoon is a dry spell (rainless period) within the rainy season, between wet spells.

stem: By roughly what date does the south-west monsoon usually cover the ENTIRE country?
solution: The south-west monsoon, after reaching the Kerala coast around 1st June, advances northward and across the country over the following weeks, and it usually covers the entire country by about mid-July (around the 15th of July). So it takes roughly six weeks to spread from the southern tip to the whole of India. (It then begins to withdraw/retreat from the north-west around early September.) Understanding that the monsoon covers all of India by mid-July is a prelims point. The south-west monsoon usually covers the entire country by about mid-July.

stem: The south-west monsoon season contributes roughly what share of India's total annual rainfall?
options: About 75% or more (the bulk of it)
solution: The south-west monsoon season (roughly June to September) contributes the overwhelming bulk of India's annual rainfall — about 75% or more (many sources say around 75–90%) of the total. This is why the south-west monsoon is so crucial for India: almost all of the country's water for agriculture, rivers, and reservoirs comes from these few monsoon months, and the success or failure of the monsoon largely determines the year's harvests and water supply. Understanding that the south-west monsoon gives ~75%+ of India's rain is a prelims point. The south-west monsoon season provides about 75% (or more) of India's total annual rainfall.

stem: Which of the following describes India's cold weather (winter) season?
options: Roughly December to February, with clear skies, low temperatures in the north, and dry conditions (except some western-disturbance rain in the NW and NE-monsoon rain on the Coromandel coast)
solution: India's cold weather (winter) season is roughly from December to February. It is characterised by: generally clear skies and fine, cool, dry weather; low temperatures in the north (which is far from the sea and gets the effect of cold northerly air), with temperatures decreasing from south to north (the south stays warm); dry conditions over most of the country (the winds blow from the land — the dry north-east monsoon). The main exceptions for rain in winter are: north-western India, which gets some rain/snow from the western disturbances; and the Coromandel coast (Tamil Nadu), which gets rain from the retreating north-east monsoon. Understanding the features of India's winter season is a prelims point. India's cold weather season (about December–February) has clear skies, low northern temperatures, and mostly dry conditions.

stem: During the hot weather (summer) season in India (March to May), a prominent feature is:
options: Rising temperatures, low pressure developing over the north-west, hot winds (Loo), and local storms (Nor'westers, dust storms)
solution: The hot weather (summer) season in India, from March to May, is characterised by: rapidly rising temperatures (the Sun moving overhead toward the Tropic of Cancer), with intense heat, especially in the north and north-west (temperatures can exceed 45°C); the development of a strong low-pressure area over the heated north-western part of the country (which will later draw in the monsoon); hot, dry, dusty winds like the Loo blowing over the northern plains; and local storms and dust storms, and the pre-monsoon thunderstorms (Nor'westers/Kalbaisakhi in the east, and mango showers in the south). It is a season of great heat, ending with the arrival of the monsoon. Understanding the features of India's summer season is a prelims point. India's hot weather season (March–May) has high temperatures, a north-western low, hot Loo winds, and local storms.

stem: One of the coldest inhabited places in India, in the Ladakh region (Kashmir), is:
solution: Drass (Dras), in the Ladakh region (Kargil district, Jammu & Kashmir), is one of the coldest inhabited places in India (and among the coldest in the world) — winter temperatures there fall far below freezing (to around −40°C or lower). This extreme cold is due to its very high altitude and its far-northern, continental, high-mountain location. This illustrates the great range of India's climate — from the freezing cold of the high north to the tropical heat of the south. Understanding that Drass is one of India's coldest places is a prelims point. Drass, in Ladakh, is one of the coldest inhabited places in India.

stem: The eastern coast of India (especially the Andhra Pradesh and Odisha coast) is frequently struck by __________ during the retreating monsoon season (October–November).
solution: The eastern coast of India — especially the coasts of Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Tamil Nadu, and West Bengal (along the Bay of Bengal) — is frequently struck by tropical cyclones during the retreating monsoon season (October–November) (and to some extent in the pre-monsoon period). These cyclones form over the warm Bay of Bengal and move toward the coast, bringing violent winds, torrential rain, storm surges, and much destruction. (The east coast is more cyclone-prone than the west coast.) Understanding that the east coast is hit by cyclones in the post-monsoon season is a prelims point. The eastern coast of India is frequently struck by tropical cyclones during the retreating monsoon season (Oct–Nov).

stem: The winter rainfall brought by western disturbances to north-western India is very important for which crop?
solution: The winter rainfall brought by the western disturbances to north-western India (Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh) is very important (highly beneficial) for the wheat crop and other rabi (winter) crops. Wheat is a rabi crop grown in the winter season, and this timely winter rain (and the moisture and cool conditions it provides) greatly helps the growth and yield of wheat in the north-western plains (the wheat belt of India). So even though this winter rain is small in amount, it is crucial for the rabi harvest. Understanding that western-disturbance winter rain benefits the wheat (rabi) crop is a prelims point. The winter rainfall from western disturbances is very important for the wheat (rabi) crop of north-western India.

stem: The reason northern India is warmer in winter than places at the same latitude in Central Asia is largely that:
options: India is closer to the Sun
The Himalayas block the cold winds from Central Asia, protecting India
solution: Northern India is warmer in winter than places at the same latitude in Central Asia largely because the Himalayas act as a barrier that blocks the extremely cold, dry winds blowing from Central Asia, preventing them from reaching India. So while Central Asia (at the same latitude, but not protected) experiences bitterly cold winters, the Himalayas shield northern India from this cold, keeping its winters much milder. This is a key example of how the Himalayas influence India's climate. Understanding this protective role of the Himalayas (warmer Indian winters) is a prelims point. Northern India is warmer in winter than Central Asia because the Himalayas block the cold Central Asian winds.

stem: Areas of India receiving very heavy rainfall (over 200 cm a year) include the west coast and the:
solution: The areas of India receiving very heavy rainfall (over 200 cm a year) include the western coast (the windward side of the Western Ghats — Kerala, coastal Karnataka, Goa, coastal Maharashtra) and the north-eastern states (Assam, Meghalaya, and the other Seven Sisters) and the sub-Himalayan region (the foothills). These areas are wet because the monsoon branches strike them and are forced to rise (orographic rain) — the Arabian Sea branch on the Western Ghats, and the Bay of Bengal branch on the north-eastern hills. (In contrast, the driest areas — under 20 cm — are western Rajasthan (Thar), Ladakh, and parts of the rain-shadow interior.) Understanding the high-rainfall regions of India is a prelims point. Areas of over 200 cm rainfall include the west coast and the north-eastern states (and sub-Himalayan belt).

stem: The 'burst' of the monsoon refers to:
options: The sudden onset of the monsoon, with an abrupt change to heavy rainfall
solution: The 'burst' of the monsoon refers to the sudden onset (arrival) of the south-west monsoon, marked by an abrupt and dramatic change from the hot, dry pre-monsoon conditions to a spell of heavy, continuous rainfall (accompanied by strong winds, thunder, and lightning, and a sharp fall in temperature). This sudden, violent beginning — as if the monsoon 'bursts' upon the land — occurs when the monsoon reaches a place (e.g., around 1st June in Kerala). It is eagerly awaited as it brings relief from the summer heat and the vital monsoon rains. Understanding the 'burst' of the monsoon (its sudden onset) is a prelims point. The 'burst' of the monsoon is its sudden onset, with an abrupt change to heavy rainfall.

stem: The warm, humid, and oppressive weather of the retreating monsoon season (in October) is popularly known as:
solution: The warm, humid, and oppressive (sultry) weather experienced during the retreating monsoon season, especially in October, is popularly known as 'October heat'. During this season, as the monsoon withdraws, the skies clear and temperatures remain high, while the ground is still moist and the air humid — producing hot, sticky, uncomfortable weather. This 'October heat' is characteristic of the transition from the rainy season to winter. Understanding 'October heat' (the sultry weather of the retreating monsoon) is a prelims point. 'October heat' is the warm, humid, oppressive weather of the retreating monsoon season in October.

stem: Which coastal region of India gets rainfall in BOTH the south-west monsoon season and (only slightly) other seasons, being on the windward side of the Western Ghats?
solution: The Malabar and Konkan coasts — the western (west-facing) coast of India — get their heavy rainfall mainly during the south-west monsoon season (June–September), because they are on the windward side of the Western Ghats, which force the moist Arabian Sea branch of the monsoon to rise and rain heavily there. (In contrast, the Coromandel coast — the south-eastern, Tamil Nadu coast — is on the leeward side during the south-west monsoon and instead gets most of its rain in winter from the retreating north-east monsoon.) Understanding that the west coast gets heavy south-west-monsoon rain is a prelims point. The Malabar/Konkan (west) coast gets heavy rainfall in the south-west monsoon, being on the windward side of the Western Ghats.

stem: The high-pressure area over the southern Indian Ocean (near the Mascarene Islands) that is the source region of the south-west monsoon winds is the __________ high.
solution: The Mascarene High is the high-pressure area that develops over the southern Indian Ocean (near the Mascarene Islands, east of Madagascar) during the northern summer. It is regarded as a source region of the south-west monsoon: the winds blow out from this southern-Indian-Ocean high, cross the equator (where they are deflected by the Coriolis force to become south-westerly), and are drawn toward the low-pressure area over the heated Indian subcontinent — becoming the moisture-laden south-west monsoon. A strong Mascarene High is associated with a strong monsoon. Understanding the Mascarene High (source of the SW monsoon) is a prelims point. The Mascarene High, over the southern Indian Ocean, is the source region of the south-west monsoon winds.

stem: The south-west direction of the summer monsoon winds (as they approach India) is due to the deflection of the cross-equatorial winds by the:
solution: The south-west direction of the summer monsoon winds (as they approach India) is due to the deflection of the winds by the Coriolis force (which arises from the Earth's rotation). The winds blowing out of the southern-hemisphere high (the Mascarene High) toward the Indian low are originally south-easterly (the south-east trade winds); as they cross the equator into the Northern Hemisphere, the Coriolis force deflects them to their right, turning them into south-westerly winds — hence the 'south-west' monsoon. So the Coriolis deflection is what gives the summer monsoon its south-westerly direction. Understanding that the Coriolis force gives the monsoon its SW direction is a prelims point. The Coriolis force deflects the cross-equatorial winds to make them south-westerly — the south-west monsoon.

stem: Which of the following is an example of the great DIVERSITY of India's climate?
options: Extremes range from the freezing cold of Ladakh/Drass to the tropical heat of the south, and from the very wet Mawsynram to the arid Thar Desert
solution: India's climate shows great diversity (regional variation), with striking extremes: in temperature, from the freezing cold of the high north (Ladakh, Drass — far below 0°C in winter) to the tropical heat of the south and the scorching summers of the north-western plains (over 45–50°C); and in rainfall, from the extremely wet Mawsynram/Cherrapunji (over 1000 cm a year) to the arid Thar Desert (under 25 cm a year). There are also great differences between coastal (equable) and interior (extreme) climates, and between the wet and dry seasons. Although India is broadly of the monsoon type, these wide regional variations make its climate very diverse. Understanding the diversity/extremes of India's climate is a prelims point. India's climate is highly diverse, ranging from the freezing cold of Ladakh to tropical heat, and from very wet Mawsynram to the arid Thar.

stem: The season that comes just before the onset of the south-west monsoon, marked by intense heat and the pre-monsoon showers, is the __________ season.
solution: The hot weather (summer) season — roughly March to May — is the season that comes just before the onset of the south-west monsoon. It is marked by intense, building heat (as the Sun moves overhead toward the Tropic of Cancer), the formation of the low pressure over north-western India, hot local winds (the Loo), and the pre-monsoon showers and storms (Nor'westers/Kalbaisakhi in the east, mango showers in the south). This season of rising heat and low pressure sets the stage for, and ends with, the arrival (burst) of the monsoon. Understanding the sequence (hot weather season precedes the monsoon) is a prelims point. The hot weather (summer) season precedes the onset of the south-west monsoon.

stem: India's climate is best classified (in the Köppen system) as predominantly a __________ type, reflecting its monsoon character.
solution: In the Köppen classification, India's climate is predominantly of the 'A' (tropical) group / monsoon type — reflecting its monsoon character (with the tropical monsoon 'Amw', tropical savanna 'Aw', etc., covering much of the country). However, India, being large and diverse, actually contains several Köppen climate types: besides the tropical (A) types over much of the country, there are dry (B) types in the Thar and rain-shadow areas, warm temperate (C) types in the north, cold (D and E) types in the high Himalayas, and so on. But the dominant, characteristic climate is the tropical/monsoon (A) type. Understanding that India is predominantly tropical/monsoon in Köppen's scheme (with variety) is a prelims point. India's climate is predominantly of the Köppen 'A' (tropical/monsoon) type, though it also contains dry, temperate, and cold types.

stem: Assertion (A): The Coromandel coast (Tamil Nadu) is dry during the south-west monsoon but wet in winter. Reason (R): It lies in the rain shadow (parallel to the wind) during the south-west monsoon, but receives rain from the retreating north-east monsoon in winter. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the Coromandel coast (Tamil Nadu) stays relatively dry during the south-west monsoon (June–Sept) but gets its main rainfall in the winter (Oct–Dec). And the reason is (R) that during the south-west monsoon, the Coromandel coast lies on the leeward/rain-shadow side (the coast runs roughly parallel to the Arabian Sea branch, and it is sheltered from the Bay branch by the land), so it stays dry; but in the winter, the retreating (north-east) monsoon winds, after picking up moisture over the Bay of Bengal, blow onto the Coromandel coast and give it rain. So R correctly explains A. Understanding this reasoning about the Coromandel coast is a prelims point. The Coromandel coast is dry in the SW monsoon (rain shadow) but wet in winter from the retreating NE monsoon.

stem: The 'Loo', 'Kalbaisakhi', and 'mango showers' are all associated with which season in India?
solution: The 'Loo' (the hot, dry wind of the northern plains), the 'Kalbaisakhi'/Nor'westers (the violent pre-monsoon thunderstorms of eastern India), and the 'mango showers' (the pre-monsoon showers of Kerala/Karnataka) are all associated with the hot weather (summer) season (roughly March–May) in India — the season of intense heat before the arrival of the monsoon. They are all pre-monsoon phenomena of this hot season. Understanding that these are all hot-weather-season features is a prelims point. The Loo, Kalbaisakhi (Nor'westers), and mango showers are all features of India's hot weather (summer) season.

stem: The seasonal reversal of monsoon winds in India is primarily driven by the differential heating and cooling of land and water. In summer, the land develops a __________ pressure area, drawing in moist oceanic winds.
solution: In summer the landmass heats rapidly and forms an intense low-pressure area over north-western India, drawing in the moisture-laden south-west monsoon from the sea.

stem: During the winter (cold weather) season, a high-pressure area develops over which region, causing dry winds to blow OUT from land towards the sea (the north-east monsoon)?
solution: In winter, a high-pressure area develops over the cold north-western/Central Asian landmass, from which dry winds blow outwards towards the sea, giving the north-east (winter) monsoon.

stem: The Indian Meteorological Department recognises four main seasons. Which of the following is the correct sequence starting from winter?
options: Cold weather → Hot weather → Advancing monsoon → Retreating monsoon
Hot weather → Cold weather → Advancing monsoon → Retreating monsoon
Advancing monsoon → Retreating monsoon → Cold weather → Hot weather
Retreating monsoon → Advancing monsoon → Hot weather → Cold weather
solution: The four seasons in order are: the cold weather season (winter), the hot weather season (summer), the advancing/south-west monsoon (rainy), and the retreating monsoon.

stem: The onset of the south-west monsoon is often sudden and violent, accompanied by thunder and lightning. This dramatic arrival is called the __________ of the monsoon.
solution: The sudden, violent onset of the south-west monsoon with heavy downpours, thunder and lightning is called the 'burst' of the monsoon.

stem: The Bay of Bengal branch of the south-west monsoon is deflected towards the north-western plains after striking which mountain range?
solution: The Bay of Bengal branch strikes the Himalayas and is deflected westward along the Ganga plains, moving progressively towards the north-west of India.

stem: Mawsynram and Cherrapunji receive extraordinarily heavy rainfall largely because the Bay of Bengal monsoon branch is trapped and forced to rise by which hills?
solution: The funnel-shaped Khasi hills of Meghalaya trap the Bay of Bengal monsoon winds and force them to rise, producing the world's heaviest rainfall at Mawsynram and Cherrapunji.

stem: The Tamil Nadu (Coromandel) coast remains relatively dry during the south-west monsoon mainly because it lies:
options: too far north of the monsoon path
parallel to the Bay of Bengal branch and in the rain shadow of the Arabian Sea branch
solution: The Coromandel coast lies parallel to the Bay of Bengal branch (so it does not intercept it) and in the rain shadow of the Arabian Sea branch, keeping it dry during the south-west monsoon; it gets rain in winter from the retreating monsoon.

stem: Roughly how many centimetres of annual rainfall is used as the boundary to define areas of 'low rainfall' (deficient) in India?
solution: Areas receiving less than about 60 cm of rainfall a year (such as western Rajasthan, Ladakh, and interior Deccan) are classed as regions of low/deficient rainfall.

stem: The Thar Desert region receives very little monsoon rainfall partly because the Aravalli range lies __________ to the path of the Arabian Sea monsoon branch, failing to obstruct it.
solution: The Aravallis lie roughly parallel to the Arabian Sea branch of the monsoon, so they do not act as a barrier to force the winds to rise; hence Rajasthan remains dry.

stem: A 'break' in the monsoon (a rainless spell during the rainy season) over northern India is often associated with the movement of the __________ away from its normal position.
solution: Breaks in the monsoon over northern India are linked to the shifting of the monsoon trough (the axis of low pressure) away from the plains, e.g. towards the Himalayan foothills.

stem: The reversal in the Walker circulation associated with El Niño weakens the Indian monsoon. The opposite phase, associated with a stronger monsoon, is called:
solution: La Niña, the cooling phase of the eastern Pacific, is generally associated with a stronger, more abundant Indian monsoon (the opposite of El Niño).

stem: The difference in sea-surface temperature between the western and eastern parts of the Indian Ocean, which also influences the Indian monsoon, is known as the:
solution: The Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) is the temperature gradient between the western and eastern equatorial Indian Ocean; a positive IOD tends to favour a good monsoon.

stem: The Tropic of Cancer passes through roughly the middle of India, meaning the southern half lies in the __________ zone and the northern half in the __________ zone.
solution: The Tropic of Cancer divides India so that the southern half lies in the tropical zone and the northern half in the sub-tropical (warm temperate) zone.

stem: At the same latitude, hill stations like Shimla are cooler than plains like Amritsar. This shows the effect of __________ on temperature.
solution: Temperature falls with height (roughly 6.5°C per 1000 m), so hill stations at high altitude are much cooler than plains at the same latitude.

stem: Coastal cities like Mumbai and Chennai have a much smaller difference between summer and winter temperatures than inland cities like Delhi and Nagpur. This moderating effect of the sea is called:
solution: The sea heats and cools slowly, moderating the temperature of nearby coasts (a small annual range). Places far inland show a large range — the continental effect.

stem: The large daily and annual range of temperature in interior northern India (very hot summers and cold winters) is an example of the __________ effect.
solution: Interior locations far from the moderating sea experience extreme heat and cold — the continental (or continentality) effect gives a large temperature range.

stem: Which of the following pressure systems, moving from west to east, brings winter rainfall to north-western India and snow to the western Himalayas?
solution: Western disturbances are extra-tropical low-pressure systems originating over the Mediterranean; they travel eastward and bring winter rain (and Himalayan snow) to north-western India.

stem: The winter rainfall from western disturbances (called 'mahawat' in the north-west) is especially beneficial for which crop?
solution: The light winter rain from western disturbances is very valuable for the standing rabi crops, particularly wheat, in the north-western plains.

stem: The withdrawal of the south-west monsoon from northern India begins around which month?
solution: The south-west monsoon begins to retreat/withdraw from the north-western plains in early September, and the process continues through October–November.

stem: During the retreating monsoon (October–November), the __________ becomes very active and receives most of its cyclonic rainfall.
solution: During the retreating monsoon, the north-east monsoon and tropical cyclones over the Bay of Bengal bring rain to the Coromandel coast of Tamil Nadu.

stem: The 'October heat' — oppressive, humid weather in the plains during the retreating monsoon — is caused by:
options: dry, cold winds from the north
high temperature combined with high humidity from the withdrawing monsoon
solution: In October the still-high temperatures combined with the humidity left by the retreating monsoon produce the muggy, uncomfortable 'October heat'.

stem: The pre-monsoon thunderstorms of Assam are locally called 'Bardoli Chheerha' because they are helpful for which crops?
solution: In Assam these storms are called 'Bardoli Chheerha' and are beneficial for tea, jute and rice cultivation.

stem: The 'Loo' is a hazard because it is a:
options: hot, dry, dusty wind of summer afternoons that can cause heatstroke
solution: The Loo is a strong, hot, dry, dusty wind blowing over the northern plains in the afternoons of May and June; prolonged exposure can be fatal (heatstroke).

stem: Dust storms accompanied by violent winds and some rain, common in the hot weather season over northern India, help to bring:
options: a fall in temperature and some relief from heat
solution: The evening dust storms of the hot season (with gusty winds and light rain) temporarily lower the temperature and bring some relief from the intense heat.

stem: The 'monsoon trough' whose position controls the distribution of monsoon rainfall over the plains is essentially an extension of the:
solution: The monsoon trough over the Ganga plains is the continental position of the ITCZ during the summer monsoon; its north-south shifts cause active and break spells.

stem: The subtropical westerly jet stream shifts to north of the Himalayas in early summer. This shift is linked to the __________ of the monsoon.
solution: The shift of the subtropical westerly jet to north of the Himalayas (and establishment of the easterly jet) coincides with the sudden onset/burst of the south-west monsoon.

stem: Which statement about the spatial distribution of rainfall in India is TRUE?
options: Rainfall generally decreases from the west coast and north-east towards the north-west interior
The desert of Rajasthan gets the most rain
Rainfall increases from the coast towards the interior
solution: Rainfall is highest on the windward west coast and the north-east and decreases towards the interior and the north-west (Rajasthan), where it is lowest.

stem: The variability of rainfall in India means that areas of LOW rainfall (like Rajasthan) tend to have __________ variability, making them prone to drought.
solution: Regions of low average rainfall generally have the highest year-to-year variability, so they are the most drought-prone.

stem: The Ganga plain shows a decreasing rainfall gradient from east to west. This is because:
options: the Bay of Bengal branch loses moisture as it moves inland north-westward
the Arabian Sea branch is strongest in the west
the plains rise in altitude to the west
western disturbances weaken to the east
solution: As the Bay of Bengal branch of the monsoon travels up the Ganga valley and turns north-west, it progressively sheds moisture, so rainfall decreases from the east to the west.

stem: Snowfall in India is generally confined to the:
options: Himalayan region and other high mountains
solution: Because of its high altitude, only the Himalayan and other high mountain regions receive snowfall; the rest of India experiences rain rather than snow.

stem: Kerala's 'mango showers' occur in which months and are important for the ripening of mangoes?
solution: Mango showers are pre-monsoon showers in Kerala and coastal Karnataka in April–May, which help mangoes to ripen.

stem: The pre-monsoon showers in Karnataka that benefit coffee plantations are locally known as the:
solution: In Karnataka these pre-monsoon showers are called 'cherry blossom' or 'coffee showers' because they help coffee flowering.

stem: The duration of the rainy (south-west monsoon) season in India is roughly:
solution: The south-west monsoon normally lasts about four months, from June to September, during which India receives the bulk of its annual rainfall.

stem: Which of the following coasts receives rainfall from the Arabian Sea branch of the south-west monsoon?
solution: The Arabian Sea branch strikes the Western Ghats and drenches the west (Konkan and Malabar) coast with heavy orographic rainfall.

stem: The moderating influence that keeps peninsular India from experiencing a well-defined cold weather season is its:
options: proximity to the sea on three sides and location near the equator
solution: Being close to the sea on three sides and near the equator, peninsular India has a maritime, near-uniform climate with no distinct winter season.

stem: Tropical cyclones forming in the Bay of Bengal during October–November most often make landfall on which coast?
options: The eastern coast (Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Tamil Nadu)
solution: Most Bay of Bengal cyclones of the retreating-monsoon season strike the eastern coast — Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and Tamil Nadu — causing heavy damage.

stem: The Palghat (Palakkad) Gap in the Western Ghats affects local climate by:
options: allowing monsoon winds and rainfall to pass through to the interior (Tamil Nadu)
solution: The Palghat Gap is a low break in the Western Ghats through which some monsoon winds can pass, influencing rainfall in the interior of Tamil Nadu.

stem: India's overall climate is described as 'monsoon type'. Countries with a similar climate are found mainly in:
solution: The monsoon type of climate characterises South and South-East Asia (India, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Thailand, etc.), where seasonal wind reversal governs the weather.

stem: In the Köppen classification, the type covering most of India (tropical with a dry season) is broadly denoted by which letter group?
solution: Most of India falls under 'A' tropical climates — 'Aw' (tropical savanna) and 'Amw' (monsoon with short dry season); the north-west desert is 'BWhw'.

stem: Which region of India, in the Köppen system, is classified as a hot desert climate ('BWhw')?
solution: Western Rajasthan (the Thar Desert) has a hot desert climate (BWhw) — very high summer temperatures and scanty, erratic rainfall.

stem: The overall UNITY that the monsoon gives to India is best expressed by the fact that:
options: every region gets the same amount of rain
the entire agricultural calendar and rural life across India revolve around the rhythm of the monsoon
the monsoon only affects the coasts
the monsoon has no economic effect
solution: Despite great regional diversity, the monsoon binds the country together because the whole agricultural year, festivals and rural economy across India depend on its seasonal rhythm.

stem: An 'inversion of temperature' in the Himalayan valleys in winter refers to the situation where:
options: the valley floor is colder than the slopes above it
the valley floor is warmer than the peaks
temperature rises with the sun only
solution: On clear, calm winter nights cold dense air drains into the valley floor, making it colder than the slopes above — an inversion of the normal decrease of temperature with height.

stem: Which combination correctly matches the local wind/phenomenon with its season?
solution: Kalbaisakhi (Norwesters) are pre-monsoon (summer) thunderstorms; the Loo is a hot summer wind, mango showers are pre-monsoon, and western disturbances bring winter rain.

stem: The El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) influences the Indian monsoon through changes in air pressure between:
options: the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal
solution: The Southern Oscillation is the see-saw of surface pressure between the eastern Pacific (Tahiti) and the western Pacific/Indian Ocean (Darwin); combined with El Niño it modulates the Indian monsoon.

stem: The intense low pressure over north-western India in summer, essential for drawing in the monsoon, is strengthened by the heating of which plateau to the north?
solution: The intense summer heating of the high Tibetan Plateau creates strong low pressure and drives the upper-air easterly jet, both of which strengthen and draw in the Indian summer monsoon.

stem: Fog is common in the northern plains during winter mornings mainly because of:
options: radiation cooling of the moist surface on clear, calm nights
solution: On clear, calm winter nights the ground cools by radiation, chilling the moist air near the surface below dew point and forming dense fog over the northern plains.

stem: Which of the following is the single most important element that makes the Indian climate distinct from other places at the same latitude?
solution: It is the monsoon — the seasonal reversal of winds bringing a concentrated rainy season — that gives India its characteristic climate, distinguishing it from other regions at similar latitudes.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Climate' (of India) is that:
options: India has a monsoon type of climate, dominated by the seasonal reversal of winds (the rain-bringing south-west summer monsoon and the dry north-east winter monsoon) caused mainly by the differential heating of land and sea, giving India its rhythm of seasons and its uneven, vital, but uncertain rainfall on which life and agriculture depend
India's climate is the same everywhere
solution: The chapter conveys that India has a monsoon type of climate, whose defining feature is the seasonal reversal of the winds through the year. This monsoon system — caused mainly by the differential heating and cooling of the vast Asian land and the surrounding seas (and influenced by the shift of the ITCZ, the Himalayas, the Tibetan Plateau, jet streams, and phenomena like El Niño) — gives India its succession of seasons: the cold weather (winter) season, when dry north-east winds blow and north-western India gets some rain from western disturbances; the hot weather (summer) season, with scorching heat and local winds like the Loo and pre-monsoon showers (Nor'westers/Kalbaisakhi in the east, mango showers in the south); the advancing (south-west) monsoon season (roughly June–September), when the moisture-laden south-west monsoon (in its Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal branches) brings the bulk of India's rainfall (very heavy on the windward west coast and the north-east, but scanty in the rain-shadow areas and the Thar Desert); and the retreating monsoon season (Sept–Nov), when the monsoon withdraws and brings rain to the Coromandel coast (and cyclones to the east coast). This rainfall is highly uneven (over space and time) and uncertain, so Indian agriculture is a 'gamble on the monsoon', yet the monsoon is also a great unifying force, binding the whole country in a shared rhythm of life. Understanding the monsoon — its cause, mechanism, seasons, and its unifying yet uncertain character — is the central concern of this chapter. India has a monsoon climate ruled by the seasonal reversal of winds, giving a rhythm of wet and dry seasons and an uneven, vital, but uncertain rainfall on which the country depends.
